concept.name: Deadlock Detection & Prevention

relationships.description: Connects Deadlock Detection & Prevention to python concurrency nogil in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Identifying and resolving circular wait conditions—where two or more threads or database transactions hold locks each other needs—via wait-for graph cycle detection, timeouts, or canonical lock ordering.
spark.keyTakeaway: Prevention via strict global lock ordering eliminates deadlocks by construction; when dynamic lock orders are unavoidable, wait-for graph cycle detection or bounded lock timeouts break the tie.

concept.whyItMatters: A deadlock freezes participating threads or database transactions permanently until external intervention. In a JVM or Go service, deadlocked worker threads exhaust the thread pool and cause cascading 504 timeouts across unrelated endpoints. In PostgreSQL or MySQL InnoDB, undetected deadlocks tie up row locks, bloat undo logs, and stall connection pools under high concurrency.
whenToUse: Multi-resource transactional updates (e.g., transferring funds between two accounts, reserving multiple warehouse SKUs) where lock acquisition order can vary across callers.
Database engines (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB) that rely on pessimistic row locks (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) under concurrent write load.
In-memory concurrent systems managing multiple mutexes, read-write locks, or resource pools.
whenNotToUse: Single-resource atomic operations that can use lock-free CAS (`AtomicLong`, `UPDATE ... WHERE version = ?`) or optimistic concurrency control.
Distributed microservices spanning multiple databases—use Sagas with idempotency and compensating actions rather than distributed pessimistic locks.
Purely immutable or actor/channel-based message-passing architectures where no shared mutexes are held across blocking calls.
keyPoints: Coffman's four necessary conditions for deadlock are Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait; breaking any single condition prevents deadlocks.
Canonical lock ordering (always locking `min(idA, idB)` before `max(idA, idB)`) breaks Circular Wait at zero runtime overhead.

Database engines build a directed **Wait-For Graph (WFG)** and run cycle detection (e.g., PostgreSQL checks after `deadlock_timeout = 1s`; InnoDB runs background/inline cycle checks) to abort the cheapest victim transaction (`40P01` / `1213`).
Lock timeouts (`innodb_lock_wait_timeout`, `SET lock_timeout = '500ms'`, `tryLock(timeout)`) bound worst-case stall duration when full cycle detection is too expensive or distributed.
Application code must catch database deadlock victim errors (`SQLState 40P01` in Postgres, `Error 1213` in MySQL) and retry the entire transaction with jittered backoff.

examples.title: Eliminating bank-transfer deadlocks via canonical lock ordering
examples.scenario: A ledger service executes concurrent transfers: Thread 1 runs `transfer(Account_A, Account_B)` while Thread 2 runs `transfer(Account_B, Account_A)` using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, triggering PostgreSQL `40P01: deadlock detected` errors at 400 TPS.
examples.outcome: Sorting account IDs before locking (`first, second = sorted([from_id, to_id])`) guarantees both transactions acquire `Account_A` before `Account_B`, reducing deadlock errors to zero.

examples.title: Preventing InnoDB gap-lock deadlocks with READ COMMITTED
examples.scenario: A high-concurrency MySQL 8.0 checkout table under default `REPEATABLE READ` suffers frequent `Error 1213` deadlocks from next-key/gap locks during concurrent `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`.
examples.outcome: Switching the session isolation level to `READ COMMITTED` (disabling gap locks for most statements) and adding a 3-attempt jittered retry handler cut failed checkouts by 99.8%.

tradeOffs.factor: Canonical Lock Ordering vs. Runtime Detection
tradeOffs.pro: Canonical ordering prevents deadlocks at compile/design time with zero victim rollbacks.
tradeOffs.con: Impossible when the second resource ID is only discovered after reading the first locked resource.

tradeOffs.factor: Wait-For Graph Detection vs. Lock Timeouts
tradeOffs.pro: WFG detection aborts deadlocks deterministically (after `1s` in Postgres) without falsely killing slow-but-healthy queries.
tradeOffs.con: Maintaining and traversing a global WFG adds CPU/lock-manager overhead under thousands of concurrent waiters.

tradeOffs.pro: Pessimistic locks prevent wasted work when contention on the same row is very high.
tradeOffs.con: Pessimistic locks risk deadlocks and hold connections open, whereas OCC (`version` column) never deadlocks.

failureModes.name: Livelock via synchronized immediate retries
failureModes.description: Two transactions deadlock, immediately abort, and retry at the exact same millisecond—repeatedly colliding and failing all retry attempts.
failureModes.mitigation: Add randomized exponential backoff with jitter (e.g., 15ms–100ms) before retrying a deadlock victim.

failureModes.name: Cross-layer mutex + DB connection pool deadlock
failureModes.description: Thread A holds an in-memory `ReentrantLock` and waits for a HikariCP connection; Thread B holds the last DB connection and waits for that same `ReentrantLock`—undetectable by PostgreSQL's WFG.
failureModes.mitigation: Never acquire or hold in-memory mutexes across blocking I/O or DB pool acquisitions, and set `connectionTimeout` + `lock_timeout`.

failureModes.name: Unbounded wait when deadlock_timeout is misconfigured
failureModes.description: Setting `deadlock_timeout` too high (e.g., 60s) leaves deadlocked transactions blocking unrelated readers and filling the connection pool.
failureModes.mitigation: Keep PostgreSQL `deadlock_timeout` at its 1s default (or 200ms–500ms for low-latency OLTP) and pair with `lock_timeout = '2s'`.

failureModes.name: False-positive timeout killing legitimate batch jobs
failureModes.description: Relying solely on an aggressive `lock_timeout = 100ms` without WFG awareness aborts valid migrations or slightly slow transactions during traffic bursts.
failureModes.mitigation: Use WFG detection for true cycles and tune `lock_timeout` comfortably above normal p99 lock hold times.

commonMistakes: Acquiring locks inside an arbitrary loop order (e.g., iterating over an unsorted `HashSet` of cart SKU IDs) instead of sorting keys first.
Retrying only the failed SQL statement inside a transaction after `40P01`/`1213` instead of rolling back and retrying the entire transaction from `BEGIN`.
Calling external HTTP APIs while holding a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` row lock, inflating lock hold times from 2ms to 2,000ms.
Assuming `deadlock_timeout = 1s` in PostgreSQL is a lock timeout; it is the *delay before running cycle detection*, not an abort timer.
Ignoring thread-dump (`jstack`) or `pg_locks` monitoring until connection pools saturate in production.

sections.content:
## The idea

A deadlock occurs when a set of two or more concurrent executions are each blocked waiting for a resource held by another member of the same set. Formally, **Coffman's four conditions** must all hold simultaneously: (1) **Mutual Exclusion** (resources cannot be shared), (2) **Hold and Wait** (a task holds one lock while requesting another), (3) **No Preemption** (locks cannot be forcibly stripped), and (4) **Circular Wait** (`T1 -> T2 -> ... -> T1`).

Systems handle deadlocks in two ways: **Prevention** breaks one of Coffman's conditions—most practically Circular Wait via **canonical lock ordering**. **Detection & Recovery** lets locks be acquired in any order, models dependencies in a **Wait-For Graph (WFG)**, and aborts a victim when a cycle forms.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace how PostgreSQL detects and resolves a circular row-lock deadlock between two concurrent transactions:

1. **Divergent acquisition**: `Tx 101` executes `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = 10` (acquires Row 10 lock). Simultaneously, `Tx 102` updates `id = 20` (acquires Row 20 lock).
2. **Cross-wait**: `Tx 101` requests `WHERE id = 20` and blocks on `Tx 102`. `Tx 102` requests `WHERE id = 10` and blocks on `Tx 101`.
3. **Wait-For Graph cycle**: After `deadlock_timeout` (default `1s`), PostgreSQL's lock manager traverses the WFG (`Tx 101 -> Tx 102 -> Tx 101`) and confirms a cycle.
4. **Victim abort**: PostgreSQL aborts `Tx 102` with `ERROR: deadlock detected (SQLSTATE 40P01)`, releasing Row 20's lock.
5. **Completion & retry**: `Tx 101` immediately acquires Row 20 and commits, while the application catches `40P01` and retries `Tx 102` after 25ms jittered backoff.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Prevention vs. Detection in real runtimes
sections.content:
## Prevention vs. Detection in real runtimes

In-memory runtimes like the **JVM** or **Go** do *not* automatically break mutex deadlocks (`synchronized`, `ReentrantLock`, `sync.Mutex`); a cycle freezes threads forever until `jstack` / `pprof` inspection or a process restart. Prevention via **canonical lock ordering** (`if idA < idB` lock `A` then `B`) or `tryLock(timeout)` is mandatory in application code.

Relational databases like **PostgreSQL** and **MySQL InnoDB** have built-in WFG detectors. PostgreSQL defers WFG traversal for `deadlock_timeout` (1s) so normal short lock waits pay zero graph-traversal CPU. InnoDB runs inline cycle detection (controlled by `innodb_deadlock_detect`) and picks the transaction that modified fewer rows as the rollback victim.

## Deadlock strategies compared

| Strategy | Mechanism | Runtime Overhead | Behavior on Contention |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Canonical Lock Ordering** | Sort resource IDs before locking | Zero | Zero deadlocks; threads wait linearly |
| **Wait-For Graph (WFG)** | Cycle detection in lock manager | Moderate (at high concurrency) | Aborts cheapest victim (`40P01` / `1213`) |
| **Bounded Lock Timeout** | `lock_timeout` / `tryLock(500ms)` | Very low | Fails fast; may abort slow non-deadlocked work |
| **Optimistic Locking (OCC)** | `WHERE version = ?` on commit | Zero lock waits | Zero deadlocks; loser retries on 0 rows updated |

## Failure modes

Under extreme contention (e.g., 500 threads hammering the same hot row in MySQL), InnoDB's `innodb_deadlock_detect` can burn 100% of CPU traversing massive wait-for graphs. High-throughput MySQL clusters sometimes disable `innodb_deadlock_detect = OFF` and rely on a short `innodb_lock_wait_timeout = 2s` instead.

In distributed systems, **cross-boundary deadlocks** (Thread A holds a Redis lock and waits on a DB row; Thread B holds the DB row and waits on the Redis lock) are invisible to both Redis and PostgreSQL. Always enforce TTLs on distributed locks and bounded timeouts on every blocking call.

## Designing deadlock-free transactions

Keep transactions short and deterministic: do all validation, JSON parsing, and external HTTP calls *before* `BEGIN`. Sort batch IDs before issuing multi-row `UPDATE` or `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` statements so every worker traverses rows in identical primary-key order.

Where multi-row locks are unavoidable, wrap the transaction boundary in a bounded retry helper (3–5 attempts with `20ms * 2^attempt + random(0, 25ms)` jitter) specifically matching `40P01` (Postgres) or `1213` (MySQL).

## Practical checklist

- Sort entity IDs canonically before acquiring multiple mutexes or `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` row locks.
- Never perform external network/HTTP I/O inside an open database transaction.
- Configure `lock_timeout` (e.g., `2s`) alongside `deadlock_timeout` (`1s`) to bound tail stalls.
- Implement full-transaction retry with exponential backoff + jitter for `SQLSTATE 40P01` / MySQL `1213`.
- Prefer optimistic concurrency (`version` column) over pessimistic locks on low-to-moderate contention paths.

interviewProblems.title: Deadlock Detection & Prevention
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Deadlock Detection & Prevention. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Identifying and resolving circular wait conditions—where two or more threads or database transactions hold locks each other needs—via wait-for graph cycle detection, timeouts, or canonical lock ordering.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Lock Manager (WFG) applies the primary invariant and coordinates with App Retry Handler.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, App Retry Handler experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Add randomized exponential backoff with jitter (e.g., 15ms–100ms) before retrying a deadlock victim.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Prevention via strict global lock ordering eliminates deadlocks by construction; when dynamic lock orders are unavoidable, wait-for graph cycle detection or bounded lock timeouts break the tie.
Avoid trap: Acquiring locks inside an arbitrary loop order (e.g., iterating over an unsorted `HashSet` of cart SKU IDs) instead of sorting keys first.
Avoid trap: Retrying only the failed SQL statement inside a transaction after `40P01`/`1213` instead of rolling back and retrying the entire transaction from `BEGIN`.
When to reach for it: Multi-resource transactional updates (e.g., transferring funds between two accounts, reserving multiple warehouse SKUs) where lock acquisition order can vary across callers.
When to reach for it: Database engines (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB) that rely on pessimistic row locks (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) under concurrent write load.

putItTogether.title: Putting Deadlock Detection Together
putItTogether.summary: Prevention via strict global lock ordering eliminates deadlocks by construction; when dynamic lock orders are unavoidable, wait-for graph cycle detection or bounded lock timeouts break the tie.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Deadlock Detection before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Sorting account IDs before locking (`first, second = sorted([from_id, to_id])`) guarantees both transactions acquire `Account_A` before `Account_B`, reducing deadlock errors to zero.
